title: O livro e a mesa — gender, articles and plurals
goal: Put *o* or *a* in front of every noun without hesitating, form plurals, and make adjectives agree — the first real hurdle for English speakers, deliberately placed at the start.
bekal: guess a noun's gender from its ending, and recognize the exceptions you must memorize
choose between *o / a / os / as* and *um / uma / uns / umas*
form plurals, including words ending in *-l*, *-m* and *-ão*

dialogs.title: Diálogo — O quarto arrendado
dialogs.intro: Budi is renting a room in Dona Fernanda's house in the Alfama district. Today he sees his room for the first time.

lines.speaker: D. Fernanda:
lines.text: Boa tarde. É o senhor Budi?
lines.id: Good afternoon. Are you Mr. Budi?
lines.literal: good afternoon. is the sir Budi?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Sou, sim. Boa tarde, dona Fernanda.
lines.id: Yes, I am. Good afternoon, Dona Fernanda.
lines.literal: I-am, yes. good afternoon, lady Fernanda.

lines.speaker: D. Fernanda:
lines.text: Este é o quarto. É pequeno, mas é confortável.
lines.id: This is the room. It's small, but it's comfortable.
lines.literal: this is the room. is small, but is comfortable.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: A janela é grande! E a cama também.
lines.id: The window is big! And so is the bed.
lines.literal: the window is big! and the bed also.

lines.speaker: D. Fernanda:
lines.text: Ali estão a mesa e uma cadeira. O armário está atrás da porta.
lines.id: Over there are the table and a chair. The wardrobe is behind the door.
lines.literal: there they-are the table and a chair. the wardrobe it-is behind of-the door.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: E a casa de banho? É no corredor?
lines.id: And the bathroom? Is it in the hallway?
lines.literal: and the house of bath? is in-the corridor?

lines.speaker: D. Fernanda:
lines.text: É. E a cozinha é ao lado. Os quartos dos outros são em cima.
lines.id: Yes. And the kitchen is next door. The other tenants' rooms are upstairs.
lines.literal: is. and the kitchen is to-the side. the(pl) rooms of-the(pl) others are on top.

lines.speaker: D. Fernanda:
lines.text: São. Duas chaves: a da porta e a do prédio.
lines.id: Yes. Two keys: the one for the door and the one for the building.
lines.literal: they-are. two keys: the of-the door and the of-the building.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: O prédio é antigo, não é?
lines.id: The building is old, isn't it?
lines.literal: the building is old, not is?

lines.speaker: D. Fernanda:
lines.text: É muito antigo. As casas de Alfama são todas antigas.
lines.id: Very old. The houses in Alfama are all old.
lines.literal: is very old. the(pl) houses of Alfama are all(f) old(f-pl).

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Thank you very much, Dona Fernanda!

notes: **O senhor Budi, a dona Fernanda.** Even titles take an article. *O senhor* and *a senhora* are the polite way to address someone you don't know well; *dona* goes before an older woman's first name, and in Portugal it sounds warm, not stiff.

**Não é?** This is the question tag for asking agreement, exactly like English "isn't it?" or "right?": *O prédio é antigo, não é?* The short form *né?* is very common in Brazil but rare in Portugal — the Portuguese say it in full.

**Da, do, no, ao — prepositions that fuse with the article.** *da porta* = *de + a porta*. *no corredor* = *em + o corredor*. *ao lado* = *a + o lado*. These contractions are **obligatory** — you can't split them — and they're fully taken apart in Unit 7. For now, just recognize them.

**Casa de banho** is "bathroom" in European Portuguese. In Brazil people say *banheiro* — a word that in Portugal means a lifeguard. This is one of the differences that most often sends learners to the wrong place.

**Todas antigas** — two words at once become plural and feminine, because *as casas* is feminine and plural. This chain of agreement is why noun gender matters: it doesn't stop at the article, it spreads to every word that describes the noun.

grammars.title: Four definite articles, four indefinite articles
body: English has just *the* and *a*. Portuguese has eight, and the choice depends on only two things: the noun's gender, and singular or plural.
after: **Portuguese uses articles far more often than English.** They appear before people's names (*o Pedro*), before country names (*o Brasil*, *a Indonésia* — but *Portugal* takes none), and before nouns in general statements: *Gosto do café* = "I like coffee", literally "I like of-the coffee".
*Uns* and *umas* mean "some", not "a-a": *uns livros* = some books.

grammars.title: Guessing gender from the ending
body: The guess is right about nine times out of ten. The rest must be memorized — and the list of exceptions you'll actually meet often turns out to be short.
after: **The exception that trips up the most learners is *o dia*.** The word for "day" ends in *-a* but is masculine, and it comes up every time you say hello: *bom dia*, not *boa dia*. Compare *boa tarde* and *boa noite*, which are both feminine.
Four Greek words ending in *-ma* are also masculine, and all are common: *o problema*, *o programa*, *o sistema*, *o tema*.
For nouns ending in *-e* there's no rule at all. Don't waste time guessing — learn them with their article the first time you meet them.

grammars.title: Plurals
body: Adding *-s* takes care of most words. Only four endings need attention.
after: **Words ending in -ão have three possible plurals**, and unfortunately all three are common: most become *-ões* (*lição → lições*), a few become *-ães* (*pão → pães*, *cão → cães*), and a few just add *-s* (*mão → mãos*, *irmão → irmãos*). Memorize those last ones; treat everything else as *-ões*.
Words already ending in an unstressed *-s* **don't change**: *o lápis* → *os lápis* (pencil), *o ónibus* → *os ónibus*. Only the article changes.

blocks.text: This is the part that feels most foreign to English speakers, because English adjectives never change. In Portuguese, an adjective **takes its form from the noun it describes** — and it usually comes **after** the noun, not before.

The good news: adjectives ending in **-e** never change for gender — and there are lots of them (*grande*, *inteligente*, *interessante*, *forte*, *simples*, *verde*). When in doubt, choosing an *-e* adjective is an honest way out.

blocks.title: Bom and mau break the pattern
items: *bom* (m) → *boa* (f) → *bons* / *boas*. Notice that the feminine isn't *boma* but *boa* — which is why *bom dia* pairs with *boa tarde*.
These two are too common to skip. Learn all four forms now.

blocks.text: Notice that every word is written with its article. Never learn one on its own.

A few words in this table may ring a bell: *a mesa* gave American English its name for a flat-topped hill (it literally means "table"), *o armário* is a cousin of *armoire*, and *o corredor* is simply a corridor. Notice, though, that each one carries a **gender** in Portuguese — something English nouns never do. Learn the article along with the word.

exercises.prompt: Write the plural, with its article.
Fill in the right form of the adjective (pequeno or pequena, novo or nova).

items: The room is small, but it's comfortable.
The key is behind the door.

answers: o — a — o — a — o — a
os livros — as lições — os hotéis — os homens — os pães — as flores
pequena — pequeno — novas — novos — boa — bom
O quarto é pequeno, mas é confortável. — A janela é grande. — As casas são antigas. — Isto é uma cadeira. — A chave está atrás da porta. — A cidade é bonita.
